Society & Human Rights
• France weighs further curfews after a weekend of violent protests, with authorities probing policing, as a suspected arson attack toppled Limoges’ historic city hall spire and luxury retailers reported looting.
• Debates over free expression and political symbolism intensified: a Calgary opera singer was dropped after raising a Palestinian flag on stage, while protests are reshaping France’s youth vote ahead of elections.
• Morocco’s first female prime minister, Fatima El Mansouri, faces competing pressures from the palace, clerics and feminists over advancing women’s rights.
• In Australia, an alleged vehicle attack critically injured MP Helen Haines, underscoring rising threats to public officials; separately, a Canadian tourist was convicted of animal cruelty after stealing a Las Vegas flamingo.
• Russell Brand’s London trial continued with a fourth accuser’s testimony alleging a “violent” assault from the early 2000s.
Why it matters: Social unrest and symbolic protests are testing democratic institutions and civil discourse, while high-profile cases and political violence highlight deepening societal strains.

Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• Alberta voters decisively rejected a path toward independence, bolstering Canadian unity and Prime Minister Mark Carney amid tensions with Washington.
• Ukraine diplomacy intensifies in Oslo, with President Zelenskyy meeting European leaders and Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, as South Korea scales back its Kyiv mission after a POW controversy.
• The US tightened tech-security lines with a ban on DeepSeek in federal agencies, while courts ordered an ex-OpenAI engineer held in custody over alleged Saudi-linked spying.
• Russia maneuvered a satellite dangerously close to ICEYE-X36 used by Ukraine, raising space-security concerns.
• Analysts note a sharp drop in President Trump’s approval ratings ahead of US midterms, and Israel faces a surge of Gen Z support for far-right parties.
Why it matters: From Canadian federalism to Ukraine peace prospects and US-China tech fissures, geopolitical fault lines are shifting amid domestic political pressures and security risks in space.
Sources: https://www.ft.com/content/8afb4e0b-302b-445c-8dde-4c5b091b808e?syn-25a6b1a6=1
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/20/zelenskyy-to-hold-peace-talks-in-oslo-with-witkoff-kushner-attending?traffic_source=rss
https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/10/russian-spacecraft-maneuvers-in-extreme-proximity-to-satellite-used-by-ukraine/

Economy & Markets
• BBC analysis shows mixed signals in the US economy under President Trump, with inflation, jobs and growth under scrutiny ahead of midterms.
• AI-linked debt risks and valuations rattled markets: South Korea’s Elice sank 32% on debut, while credit default swap trading tied to big tech surged as investors hedged against an AI unwind.
• Revolut suffered a broad “service disruption” affecting payments and withdrawals, though it said funds and data remained safe.
• Global commodities tightness persists: Codelco set a record $350/ton premium for European copper; FT reported Iran-related disruptions shifting oil power toward the Americas.
• India’s Jio Platforms targets a massive IPO amid a volatile market, and banks warn not all data centers will be viable even in an AI boom.
Why it matters: Markets are grappling with AI exuberance and leverage, fintech reliability, and commodity supply shocks that could shape inflation and investment flows.
Sources: https://www.ft.com/content/6dd31584-064c-4015-bf5d-e5747799ccd5?syn-25a6b1a6=1

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv98ze40jz18o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss

Armed Conflict & Security
• Albania entered a seventh day of violent anti-government clashes, with nearly 300 injured, over half of them police.
• Australia confronted rising threats to politicians after MP Helen Haines was critically injured in an alleged targeted car attack; charges were filed against a suspect.
• The UK will deploy jets to help defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi strikes, signaling deeper security cooperation.
• Cyber risk remains acute: attackers are exploiting unpatched Plex media servers to install malware.
Why it matters: Political violence, regional military tensions, and persistent cyber vulnerabilities underscore a broadening security landscape straddling streets, skies, and networks.
Sources: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy4xjlpqgd3o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
https://www.ft.com/content/59a3252c-3ea6-4e1e-bcc7-fef15cce16da?syn-25a6b1a6=1

Health & Pandemic
• Pennsylvania issued a rare alert for congenital measles, a potentially fatal condition not seen in the US for decades.
• US communities battle the “tranq” crisis as synthetic opioids like fentanyl reshape drug landscapes.
• New orexin-agonist drugs for narcolepsy could have broader therapeutic potential, while technologists highlight improved tracking of foodborne pathogens amid rising public concern.
• Bloomberg reports a booming black market for GLP‑1 drugs in Brazil, fueling crime and public health risks.
Why it matters: Emerging disease threats, synthetic drug epidemics, and access to powerful therapies are testing public health systems and regulatory oversight.
Sources: https://arstechnica.com/health/2026/10/pennsylvania-issues-alert-on-congenital-measles-something-us-hasnt-seen-for-decades/
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cqd097z3epvno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss

Climate & Environment
• The strongest El Niño on record is reshaping global weather patterns; New Zealand’s climate enters “uncharted territory” with more extremes ahead.
• Reports warn it may become harder to hold countries accountable on emissions as climate assessment timelines stall; IPCC authors pledge to press on despite political deadlock.
• Marine life in the Gulf of Mexico fell ~60% in deep zones after the BP spill, new research finds; Europe’s wild bees also continue long-term decline.
• Companies ramp fossil power amid slowing renewables growth; Amazon backs a new nuclear plant in Indiana; startups test underwater geothermal; batteries’ production emissions remain a focus.
• Wildlife crossings show promise: a Colorado overpass cut vehicle-animal collisions by 91%.
Why it matters: Climate volatility, biodiversity declines, and energy-system trade-offs are accelerating, demanding credible policy, reliable low‑carbon power, and nature-centric infrastructure.
Sources: https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c6dx07dznpyyo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss

Sports
• UEFA demanded FIFA disclose documents tied to an abandoned World Cup “sell-off” plan, sending 42 questions and setting a Nov. 2 deadline.
• England Rugby League defended its World Cup preparation as it seeks to steady its campaign; Wales made changes ahead of facing Samoa.
• The San Francisco 49ers stayed unbeaten at 6-0 after beating Washington 23-17; PSG face Barcelona in a marquee Champions League tie.
Why it matters: Governance transparency and on-field performance are shaping fan trust, competitive integrity, and the business of global sport.

Science & Technology
• Japan launched its MMX mission to return samples from Mars’ moon Phobos by 2029, while NASA closed out the OSIRIS‑REx mission phase as scientists continue analyzing Bennu samples.
• Samsung’s massive Pyeongtaek memory hub ramps to meet AI-era demand; European carriers plan a Starlink alternative for direct-to-device satellite service.
• A Florida DMV data breach exposed residents’ data after a police department stored logins insecurely; ReactOS reached a milestone with NTFS install support.
• NASA advances shock and vibration analysis for spacecraft, while new research spotlights quantum error-correction gains and a neutrino mass experiment in China.
Why it matters: Space exploration, resilient infrastructure, and advances in computing and communications underpin the next wave of scientific discovery and industrial capability.
Sources: https://arstechnica.com/space/2026/10/japan-launches-mission-to-bring-home-a-piece-of-the-martian-moon-phobos/

Artificial Intelligence
• AI finance jitters deepened as CoreWeave’s bonds slipped into distressed territory, fueling broader questions about private credit in AI infrastructure.
• Microsoft warned enterprises that AI agents can resemble insider threats and urged tighter oversight; hackers breached OpenCode to steal API keys, running up users’ AI bills.
• Amazon introduced TorchNeuron to loosen Nvidia’s grip on PyTorch; Tenstorrent raised $1.5B to scale open‑weight AI chips; Otter.ai secured $320M in growth funding.
• Policy debates surged: Democrats eye stricter AI regulation if they gain Congress; embedded evaluators and safety governance remain contentious; Germany urged businesses to “open doors for AI.”
• Researchers claimed progress on AI proofs (Quasi‑Riemann), agentic AI for heterogeneous systems, and cross‑disciplinary science tools, while concerns rose over AI-powered hacking and game cloning.
Why it matters: The AI boom’s capital structure, security risks, competitive hardware landscape, and regulatory responses will determine how safely and broadly AI’s benefits are realized.

Entertainment
• Apple set an Oct. 28 event widely expected to unveil new Macs and a refreshed iPad mini, as analysts speculate about a touchscreen laptop.
• Disney named Carol Choi president of Asia Pacific as Luke Kang retires; financiers launched a €100M fund to support Italy’s indie film sector.
• Box office: “Street Fighter” opened atop the UK/Ireland charts; Rajinikanth’s “Jailer 2” debuted third; new “Blade Runner 2099” trailer teased cosmic visuals.
• Music highlights included Cardi B’s acclaimed Tiny Desk, MUNA safely escaping a tour-bus fire, and 82WORLD’s LA festival moments; legal news saw Mariah Carey prevail in a defamation suit.
Why it matters: Platform launches, industry leadership changes, and new financing are reshaping media strategies, while strong content and live events continue to anchor audience engagement.

Art & Culture
• Egyptian documentary “Big Boys Don’t Cry” probes masculinity among Cairo bodybuilders and bouncers; “Lex Julia” offers a post-#MeToo island-set suspense narrative from Estonia-Finland.
• Brooklyn honored the late Billy Jones of Baby’s All Right with a street renaming; KAWS designed a limited-edition Absolut Vodka bottle.
• Marina Abramović released “Long Life, Short Stories,” an illustrated reflection on memory and creation; Paulin and Hodinkee unveiled a vintage‑inspired Mara watch.
Why it matters: New works and commemorations reflect evolving cultural conversations about gender, consent, memory, and design, linking contemporary art to community identity.
Sources: https://variety.com/2026/film/global/big-boys-dont-cry-muhammad-mustapha-el-gouna-1236916813/

Longevity & Anti-Aging
• Researchers reported preliminary results from a first-in-human partial epigenetic reprogramming trial, aiming to restore youthful cell states without dedifferentiation risks.
• Studies explored cellular senescence in liver aging and an RNA regulator (MTR4) that mitigates endothelial DNA damage; evidence for peroxisome dysfunction’s role in Alzheimer’s remains inconclusive.
Why it matters: Interventions targeting aging hallmarks—from epigenetics to senescence—are advancing toward clinical reality, with careful validation needed to balance promise and safety.

Society & Human Rights.title: Federal efforts over alleged noncitizen voting escalate with California arrests | First Thing
Society & Human Rights.text: The DoJ has charged 28 green card holders in California, accusing them of fraudulently registering to vote. Plus, is the world really ready for AI actors?Good morning. The US Department of Justice has charged 28 green card holders in California, accusing them of fraudulently registering to vote and casting illegal ballots. The arrests – 11 people are in custody – mark the latest escalation in federal efforts against alleged noncitizen voting.The crackdown comes days after the DOJ sued California to block the state from tabulating certain ballots in November’s midterms. California’s secretary of state, Shirley Weber, called the demands “outrageous”, pointing out that federal officials have spent months making “vague and unsubstantiated allegations”. Democrats and voting rights groups say the administration is laying the groundwork to sow doubt over November’s election results.How are Congress members being targeted before the midterms? More than three dozen members of US Congress have had their offices targeted with envelopes containing white powder, less than three weeks before the election, as federal agents try to identify who is behind the campaign.What has Donald Trump said about the French protests? At a rally in Kansas Trump described France as a once-great nation that had been “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists”. Earlier in the day, Trump repeated his baseless claim that migrants had “taken over” France, and also claimed that “Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon”. Society & Human Rights.title: IEEE Report Highlights How Members Are Engineering for Public Good
Society & Human Rights.text: Advancing technology for the benefit of humanity isn’t just the tagline for IEEE’s mission as a public charity. It’s something that the organization’s more than 500,000 members strive to do all the time. IEEE’s recently released 2025 Social Impact Report showcases a variety of programs volunteers worked on to increase public awareness of technology’s impact on society, many of which The Institute covered.Here is a selection of the programs from the report, with links to our related articles: Shaping trustworthy digital experiences for children online. An IEEE collaboration with Indonesian policymakers led to a new regulation to protect children, a first of its kind in the region. The advanced frameworks used for the design of Internet platforms and systems are based on the IEEE 2089-2021 and 2089.1-2024 standards. The IEEE 2089-2021 Standard for an Age-Appropriate Digital Services Framework Based on the 5Rights Principles for Children provides practical steps to qualify online products and services. The follow-up, the IEEE 2089.1-2024 Standard for Online Age Verification, provides a framework for designing, specifying, evaluating, and deploying age-verification systems. You can learn more about the two standards in “IEEE Makes Strides to Improve Online Safety for Kids.”Catalyzing humanitarian outreach. Last year IEEE launched its Mobile Outreach Vehicle (MOVE) program in India. The vehicle brings educational resources to communities and can provide communication and technology support to relief workers and survivors during emergencies. In 2024, for example, MOVE helped survivors of Hurricanes Helene and Milton in the Southeastern United States. When the vehicles are not deployed, IEEE MOVE remains engaged in outreach efforts, participating in 25 STEM educational events such as one in San Diego in 2023.Preserving Tech History. The IEEE Global Museum, developed by the IEEE History Center, presents traveling exhibits to educate the public about the history of technology and its impact on society. In “IEEE’s Global Museum Brings Engineering History to You,” you can learn about current exhibits “Unseen Signals: E. Howard Armstrong’s Radio Revolution” and “Microchips That Shook the World.”EPICS in IEEE. This program provides nonprofit organizations with technology solutions while broadening undergraduate students’ hands-on experiences. Last year US $290,000 was awarded to a record-breaking number of service projects around the world. Among the 48 projects was one in which a student team in Macedonia created IoT-driven sensing and display devices to help measure and promote awareness of pollution and air-quality issues in the capital city of Skopje.IEEE TryEngineering. This initiative inspires preuniversity students to pursue technology and engineering careers. It awarded US $70,379 in grants to 58 programs around the world. One is its TryEngineering Summer Institute, a nine-day summer sleepaway camp for students ages 13 to 17. More than 310 students participated last year, learning about aerospace and artificial intelligence.IEEE–Eta Kappa Nu. IEEE-HKN has more than 260 collegiate chapters worldwide and more than 200,000 members. The honor society encourages and recognizes excellence in education, professional practice, and meritorious work within IEEE’s designated fields of interest. IEEE-HKN members last year contributed 110,442 volunteer hours to universities and communities, and they held 827 service and outreach events and 137 STEM outreach activities. Last year IEEE and HKN celebrated the 15th anniversary of their merger.IEEE Connecting the Unconnected Challenge. This annual global competition solicits innovative solutions from startups, grassroots organizations, universities, and others working to bridge the digital divide. The Institute wrote about last year’s winners. They included a solar-powered community broadband network in Tanzania, a low-cost method for accessing the Internet that uses FM radio and a short message service, and a strategy for utilizing India’s rural broadband infrastructure to deliver medical services to people living in isolated, tribal, and other underserved regions.Supporting Sustainable Climate Efforts. IEEE helps foster the exchange of technical knowledge and information to develop technologies for a sustainable climate. “IEEE Plays a Pivotal Role in Climate Mitigation Talks” reported how the organization enhanced its standing as a trusted, neutral authority on the role of technology in climate change mitigation and adaptation. Leaders, including 2023 IEEE President Saifur Rahman, showcased tech solutions at COP30 and the International Symposium on Achieving a Sustainable Climate. Also, “IEEE Young Professionals Talked Sustainability Tech at Climate Week NYC” reported on the group’s activities during the 2024 Climate Week NY, the largest annual climate event, featuring more than 600 activities throughout New York City.Engineering: A force for good“The IEEE global community of more than 500,000 members and volunteers demonstrates what is possible when expertise is mobilized for the public good,” Sophia Muirhead, IEEE executive director and chief operating officer, said in a news release about the Social Impact Report. “Technology has the power to expand opportunity, strengthen communities and improve lives, and IEEE’s mission is to ensure that this power is used responsibly, ethically, and in service of humanity. The 2025 report shows how IEEE members and volunteers are advancing solutions that make a real difference in people’s lives around the world.”Engagement research shows that members increasingly cited “giving back to my profession and the world community” as a reason for joining IEEE and renewing their membership, IEEE President Mary Ellen Randall said in her September column about the report.“Humanitarian programs are not only meaningful,” she wrote. “They also are magnetic. They attract younger engineers, keep them engaged, and help them build a professional identity rooted in purpose and impact.“IEEE has the opportunity to become the world’s leading convening force for developing interdisciplinary technology solutions to solve humanity’s most important challenges. Our future relevance will be defined not only by the technologies we advance but also by the problems we choose to help solve.”

Science & Technology.text: Agility Robotics, the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5. It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do.Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined.From ATRIAS to DigitMy dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals.We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS—short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait.With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be? Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones, and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie.Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them. ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year.Agility RoboticsBecause Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash.Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1, which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers.Why Digit Began With Warehouse BinsAs we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers. After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins. Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation. Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills.In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company, we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO. In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine. Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could.I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact.Turning Digit Into a ProductI knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary. Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. AgilityWe had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities. While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction.Christie Hemm Klok I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move.Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned.Digit 5Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements. Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can.Christie Hemm KlokCustomer requirements helped us realize that safety in particular was one of the most critical barriers to scaling. In Digit 4’s commercial deployments, the robots had to work behind physical barriers, separated from humans at all times, to meet insurance and regulatory demands. This seemed silly to me, because I’ve never felt that our robots were dangerous, but we have to prove that they’re safe. And since keeping the robots in safety cages severely limited their usefulness, enabling Digit 5 to operate safely around people became a primary design goal. We spent two years on this challenge.Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers. It will rely on an array of sensors to locate nearby people in a manner that’s certifiably safe, and then take actions based on that information. As a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop what it’s doing, set down its payload, sit on the floor, and cut power to its motors before the person gets close enough to touch the robot. This conservative approach reduces the risk to nearby people in a verifiable way, and we believe it’s the only approach that makes sense as a first step toward working alongside humans. Yet this strategy also feels like a massive slowdown on the path toward robots becoming part of everyday life. Enabling coexistence with humans has influenced almost every aspect of Digit 5’s design: the shape of the legs and the body, the safety-rated sensors within protective housings, the isolated computers dedicated to safety, and more. All of these features increase the robot’s complexity, power consumption, mass, and physical size.  Digit 5 is Agility’s largest, heaviest, strongest, and most capable humanoid robot worker.  The robot’s design was driven by safety, with integrated protection for the robot and for the humans it will work around.Agility RoboticsWeighing over 120 kg, Digit 5 is a huge robot. It needed to achieve the lifting limits recommended under the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health guidelines for human workers, which include repeatedly lifting 23-kg bins and reaching shelves 1.75 meters high. Digit is designed to perform tasks like these for 20 hours a day—something no human can do. This requires motors with enough power and torque to lift the load, but also enough precision to delicately control the force Digit applies when it makes contact with the world. To power those motors, we needed a large battery and a dock for rapid autonomous charging. The dock will deliver 240 amperes at 48 volts, which is enough current to make its thick charging cables visibly wiggle under the induced magnetic forces, while powerful fans blow air through cooling channels in the robot’s torso to keep the battery from overheating. The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso, but it will allow the robot to operate for 90 minutes and fully recharge during a 9-minute break, enabling near-continuous work.All of this extra bulk means that Digit 5 can no longer run or jump the way previous generations could, and the svelte form I imagined has become physically impossible. In some ways, Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build. But looking at the situation rationally, I believe this trade-off is necessary for any company that claims its humanoid can do this kind of work today: If you see a robot that looks like a human working in a factory or warehouse, it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift. And if it’s not covered with sensors, it’s likely not safe to stand next to.The most visible change with Digit 5 is that humanlike legs replace the ostrichlike legs of our earlier versions. While the “backward” leg configuration was optimized for walking and running, we discovered that it created problems with squatting because the ankle will strike the ground. Digit 5 will spend a lot of time lifting heavy objects from near the floor, so we used a humanoid leg configuration with knee and hip motors that both contribute torque to help the robot stand up again.  When Digit detects an approaching human, the robot will lower itself to the floor and cut power to its motors. Agility believes this is the only near-term approach to verifiably reduce risk when the robot is working near people.Agility RoboticsOther companies building humanoid robots have copied the human form without ever understanding its purpose. It’s very frustrating that, to an outside observer, it now looks like we discarded Agility’s distinctive leg design and simply did what everyone else was doing. Yet I know that we arrived at this shape based purely on functional engineering choices. Making a robot look like a human is the easy part—without the function to match, and the understanding of the physics underlying that function, the whole point of the human form may be lost.With the power, battery life, and safety features that we are designing into Digit 5, we will have a truly useful robot. But it also compromises on some things that are core to my vision and mission. I understand why we made the choices we did and can justify them all, but together they leave me unsatisfied. It’s the curse of the engineer.What Comes After Digit 5I believe Digit 5 will be the scaling moment for Agility Robotics, the inflection point where we can begin deploying robots in large numbers. While the robot will continue carrying bins, our road map includes many more tasks, from picking individual items and tending machines, to preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually doing assembly work itself. Its interchangeable tool interfaces and modular design will enable us to gradually upgrade its subsystems. It will be a platform for improvement, a source of data for future behavior training, and a viable product all at the same time.  Hurst stands between the previous version of Digit, Digit 4 EVT [left], and Digit 5.Christie Hemm KlokBut I cannot love Digit 5. It’s the largest, heaviest, most expensive robot Agility will ever build, full of design compromises that enable it to be exactly the robot it needs to be right now rather than the robot I dreamed of. In the beginning, I envisioned steady progress on agility and dexterity, with each version becoming more dynamically capable. Instead, developing Digit 5 has required large detours to incorporate requirements that seemed unrelated to my original vision. However, I now recognize that tackling these challenges was always necessary. Customers and product requirements didn’t ruin my vision; they revealed what my vision was missing. This is how robots will achieve commercial success and make a real-world impact, which will bring me closer to my scientific dream as well.We won’t have a humanoid that matches the capabilities of humans until it achieves that mastery of motion that inspired me to found Agility over a decade ago. I saw glimmers of it with the spring-mass locomotion of ATRIAS, and more glimmers with Cassie’s running gait.I know that such mastery is physically possible with the tools and hardware that we have right now, and despite all of its compromises, Digit 5 will give us a practical foundation for pursuing that dream. I want every future version of Digit to be lighter and more graceful, to interact more naturally with humans, and to be better at manipulating objects and moving through the world, enabling robots to enter aspects of our lives that they haven’t been able to help with before. By the time I’m old enough to need assistance at home, I expect Digit will be up to the task.With Digit 5, Agility has built a robot that will be useful in our world. Now I’m getting back to work to make it beautiful, too.

Entertainment.title: Blauer’s New Season Collection Is Made for Winters in the City
Entertainment.text: This season, Blauer elevates its technical apparel to support active city lifestyles. As captured in its latest campaign, featuring UK music artists DYLAN, Cassyette, and Ben Kidson, the new collection aims to provide contemporary style without sacrificing core functionality.In contrast to last season’s rugged, outdoors-ready clothing, the Fall/Winter 2026 range takes on a sharper look throughout its four lines: B Department, B Essential, B Project, and B. Urban Police. A staple for the cooler months, the down jacket is reworked in new ways, including a casual wave-quilted jacket, a thermoregulating graphene version, and a unique semi-transparent ripstop piece with visible feathers. To accentuate the sleek aesthetic, the brand also delivers leather jackets in biker, pilot, and military-inspired cuts. The varied silhouettes adapt Blauer’s heritage styles with washed treatments and a versatile color palette of “Black Ink,” “London Fog,” “Total Eclipse,” and “Peat.” For much-needed winter layering, these jackets drop alongside ribbed jumpers and polo knits. Elsewhere, the new collection also features a special edition B.Cortina capsule. Designed more specifically for mountain escapes, the range offers thermal jackets and a coordinated outerwear set, both adorning a Queen of the Dolomites-inspired print. You can now check out the pieces in the new campaign lensed by Bryan Adams. Adopting Blauer’s signature black-and-white aesthetic, he frames the contemporary feel of the garments while highlighting the cast’s unmistakable individuality. Entertainment.title: The Salomon XT-6 PROTECTIVE and XT-WHISPER GTX Receive BILLY’S-Exclusive Colorways
Entertainment.text: Name: Salomon XT-6 PROTECTIVE & XT-WHISPER GTX BILLY’s ExclusivesColorway: Stormy Weather/Dark Navy/Trooper, Grisaille/Dark Navy/BlackSKU: TBCMSRP: ¥26,400 - ¥29,700 JPY (approx. $167 - $188 USD)Release Date: October 23Where to Buy: BILLY’s TokyoSalomon continues to blur the lines between rugged outdoor performance and urban streetwear with a newly unveiled footwear capsule arriving exclusively at BILLY'S. The drop reimagines two of the French brand's most celebrated technical silhouettes - the XT-6 PROTECTIVE and the XT-WHISPER GORE-TEX - in mood-evoking, weather-ready colorways. Designed to adapt effortlessly to both city streets and unpredictable natural environments, the collection beautifully balances cutting-edge utility with a sophisticated.The XT-6 PROTECTIVE takes the darker, more utilitarian route, replacing the model’s usual technical mesh emphasis with a ripstop upper inspired by workwear. Its "Stormy Weather" base reads as a muted blue-grey, overlaid with pale Trooper green-grey SensiFit lines that trace the sidewalls and toe before giving way to Dark Navy and black around the heel and heavily lugged sole. The silhouette specifically highlights the interplay between matte and glossy finishes, which creates extra depth across the layered upper, while a visible GORE-TEX tab signals the shoe’s weather-resistant construction. Entertainment.title: MAMMUT and BEAMS Revive the Expedition-Proven “Serac Extreme Jacket” for a Limited Run
Entertainment.text: SummaryBEAMS is reissuing MAMMUT’s Serac Extreme Jacket as a limited special edition built closely on the original designThe updated shell uses GORE-TEX and pairs a large MAMMUT logo on one sleeve with BEAMS embroidery on the otherA sweatshirt and cap arrive alongside the jacket to complete the releaseMAMMUT and BEAMS are reviving the Swiss outdoor brand’s Serac Extreme Jacket through the “SERAC EXTREME JACKET BEAMS SPECIAL,” a limited reissue that stays faithful to the original while folding in present-day performance and BEAMS-exclusive touches. The shell carries real expedition credentials, having protected climber Stephan Siegrist through harsh conditions during his December 1995 push into the peaks of Patagonia.The jacket’s pattern sticks closely to the first-generation Serac Extreme, keeping the overall shape that earned it a reputation in alpine circles. Rather than chase a full redesign, the reissue upgrades what sits beneath the surface, with a GORE-TEX build bringing the waterproof, weather-blocking protection expected from a modern hardshell.Branding is split across the sleeves to reflect the partnership. An oversized MAMMUT logo runs along the left arm, while the right sleeve carries embroidered BEAMS lettering, giving each label its own side of the jacket without crowding the body.Some of the most considered details sit on the inside. The lining features a special “EIGER STORY LABEL” produced for this edition, joined by a revived MAMMUT brand label that nods to the jacket’s original era. The launch also includes a sweatshirt and a cap, extending the reissue beyond outerwear for those who want the look in lighter layers.The MAMMUT x BEAMS “SERAC EXTREME JACKET BEAMS SPECIAL,” along with the accompanying sweatshirt and cap, drops on Friday, October 23 at select BEAMS stores and via the BEAMS online store.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Glossy black mudguards and sculpted black Air tooling give the pair a harder technical edge, while small Yellow Ochre details on the outsole add an unexpected warm accent beneath the otherwise dark build.Meanwhile, the Shox TL “Black/Tough Red/Yellow Ochre/Black” uses the same plaid textile beneath a black skeletal cage, paired with glossy black Shox columns and a dark leather heel for the most overtly Y2K treatment of the four. Entertainment.title: Acqua di Parma’s Holiday 2026 Collection Is a Colorful Celebration of Italian Hospitality
Entertainment.text: SummaryAcqua di Parma unveils its Holiday 2026 collection, designed with Italian artist Agostino Iacurci.Inspired by the fictional Grand Hotel Sprezzatura, the collection features sculptural ceramics, festive fragrances and an Advent Calendar.Prices range from $65 to $1,022 USD.For this holiday season, Acqua di Parma is inviting guests to check into the fictional Grand Hotel Sprezzatura, an imaginative alpine retreat where Italian hospitality, theatrical storytelling and festive fragrance converge. Celebrating its 110th anniversary, the Italian fragrance house has collaborated with multidisciplinary artist Agostino Iacurci to create a colorful visual universe inspired by the Dolomites and the effortless elegance of sprezzatura, the Italian art of making even the most elaborate gestures appear natural.Drawing on the theatrical traditions of Commedia dell'Arte, Iacurci imagines a cast of hotel characters whose personalities unfold through bold geometric compositions. Inspired by the modular logic of Tangram puzzles, his illustrations combine architectural facades, mountain silhouettes, expressive masks and playful human figures, transforming the collection's packaging into a series of interconnected visual stories. Rendered in vibrant yellows, oranges, blues and earthy tones, the designs reinterpret Acqua di Parma's signature aesthetic through a festive, surrealist lens, capturing the warmth and eccentricity of an imaginary Italian mountain getaway.At the heart of the collection is a series of limited-edition Masterpiece objects named after the hotel's fictional protagonists, Alfredo, Clementina and Tobia. Handcrafted and painted in Tuscany, the ceramic creations encompass refillable fragrance bottles, candles and diffusers, distinguished by stacked geometric forms, sculptural finials and character-inspired silhouettes. Produced in editions of just 200 pieces, each object bears Iacurci's signature alongside the Maison's branding. The wider holiday assortment introduces seasonal home fragrances in Bosco, Panettone and Torrone, evoking the atmosphere of an Italian winter through references to woodland landscapes and traditional festive sweets.Candles and diffusers arrive in decorated glass vessels featuring distressed gold-leaf detailing, while three signature fragrances - Colonia Il Profumo, Buongiorno and Zafferano - receive special Designer Edition packaging. A particularly elaborate highlight is the Advent Calendar, reimagined as a miniature Grand Hotel Sprezzatura with stacked cylindrical architecture, opening windows and illustrations of snowy trees, alpine scenery and eccentric hotel guests. Additional gift sets span the Colonia, Blu Mediterraneo, Buongiorno and Signatures of the Sun collections, offering a selection of fragrances, candles and personal care essentials.Extending beyond fragrance, the Holiday 2026 collection introduces two Italian-made design objects under Acqua di Parma's Art of Living line. The Olé Pocket Comb & Mirror pairs tortoiseshell resin accessories with a tan calfskin leather charm and signature yellow resin sphere, while the Decidi Tu Polyhedric Glass Object is crafted from mouth-blown borosilicate glass and designed for multiple uses, including holding stick candles, matches or fragrance diffuser reeds.Prices range from $65 USD for the 70-gram Bosco Candle to $1,022 USD for the Advent Calendar. Art & Culture.title: Marina Abramović Turns Eight Decades of Life Into ‘Long Life, Short Stories’
Art & Culture.text: SummaryMarina Abramović reflects on memory, creativity and personal philosophy in Long Life, Short Stories.The illustrated volume blends drawings, anecdotes and introspection.Published by Rizzoli Electa, the 224-page book is priced at $65 USD.Marina Abramović turns inward for Long Life, Short Stories, a new illustrated volume that reframes one of performance art’s most uncompromising careers through memories, drawings and personal reflection. The book unfolds as what its publisher, Rizzoli Electa, describes as part sketchbook, part diary and part personal philosophy, moving through subjects including love, sex, loss, fear, nature, ancestry, creativity, dreams and even love spells. The fragmented format feels particularly suited to an artist whose practice has long used lived experience as material, offering a more intimate counterpart to the endurance, vulnerability and physical risk that have defined her public work.Published as Abramović celebrates her 80th birthday in 2026, the book arrives at another significant point in a career that helped establish performance art as a major contemporary discipline. Since emerging in the early 1970s, the Serbia-born artist has repeatedly tested the physical and psychological boundaries between performer and audience, from early works including Rhythm 0 and Rhythm 5 to her landmark 2010 Museum of Modern Art retrospective The Artist Is Present. Long Life, Short Stories approaches that history from a deliberately different angle. Original drawings created for the publication sit alongside direct, often humorous accounts and philosophical observations, revealing some of the emotional and psychological terrain behind works more commonly discussed through ideas of endurance, time, presence and bodily limits.The book is less a chronological autobiography than a loosely assembled map of Abramović’s inner world, shifting between the mystical, provocative and unexpectedly everyday while allowing personal episodes to sit alongside broader reflections on creativity and human connection. It also adds a more private dimension to a milestone year that includes major projects surrounding her 80th birthday, including a large-scale presentation at New York’s Park Avenue Armory.Marina Abramovic: Long Life, Short Stories spans 224 pages in hardcover and is priced at $65 USD via Rizzoli. Abramović will also mark the release at Rizzoli Bookstore in New York on October 29 with a conversation alongside Michèle Lamy centered on artistic freedom, the expressive possibilities of the body and a life spent creating beyond convention.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Art & Culture.title: Paulin’s Mara Gets a Genuine Galvanic Gilt Dial for Hodinkee
Art & Culture.text: SummaryPaulin and Hodinkee rework the Mara with a vintage-inspired gilt dial and aged lume.The limited edition uses a slimmer 11.8mm case and Miyota 9039 automatic movement.Limited to 250 pieces, it is priced at $1,000 USD.Paulin and Hodinkee have teamed up on a limited edition of the Mara, revisiting the Glasgow watchmaker’s first dive watch through the lens of mid-century tool watches. Founded in 2013 and operating alongside sister brand anOrdain, Paulin has built its identity around expressive color, typography and playful modern design, but the Mara Limited Edition for Hodinkee takes a deliberately more archival direction. Its 39.7mm stainless-steel cushion case retains the architecture of the standard Mara, while the dial trades Paulin’s usual geometric markers for classic diver indices, warm gilt accents and antiqued Super-LumiNova inspired by the black-and-gold dive watches of the 1950s and early ’60s.The defining feature is its genuine galvanic gilt dial, produced using a traditional process rather than simply printing gold-colored details onto a black surface. Each brass dial is first electroplated in gold before the minute track, logos and lettering are masked with a chemical resist; a subsequent galvanic treatment turns the exposed areas matte black, leaving the underlying gold visible through the markings. Paulin then hand-paints the hour markers with aged-tone Super-LumiNova to match the hands and bezel scale. Other period-minded touches include the meters-first depth rating, a gilt Hodinkee signature at 4 o’clock and Paulin’s custom Wim typeface, while a dark grey 120-click bezel uses a double-domed sapphire insert. A black-and-grey striped NATO strap with a Hodinkee-signed buckle completes the vintage-informed treatment.Inside, the collaboration swaps the Swiss movement used by the standard production Mara for a Miyota 9039 automatic calibre, providing a 42-hour power reserve while helping slim the case from 13.5mm to 11.8mm. Water resistance has correspondingly been reduced from 300 meters to a still practical 100 meters, creating proportions closer to vintage skin divers while retaining modern features including sapphire construction and a screw-down crown.Limited to 250 individually numbered pieces, the Paulin Mara Limited Edition for Hodinkee is priced at $1,000 USD and is available for pre-order through Hodinkee and Watches of Switzerland, with deliveries expected to begin in mid-November 2026.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Longevity & Anti-Aging.title: Cellular Senescence in Liver Aging
Longevity & Anti-Aging.text: Senescent cells accumulate with age, perhaps primarily because the aged immune system becomes less able to efficiently destroy senescent cells as it does in youth. When a cell becomes senescent it ceases to replicate, grows in size, and secretes a potent mix of pro-inflammatory, pro-growth signals that contribute to the chronic inflammation of aging and are disruptive to tissue structure and function.
